summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct has been decriminalised in Fiji since the Crimes Act 2010 came into force on 1 February 2010, repealing the colonial-era Penal Code offence that carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement of that offence was documented into 2005: in April of that year two men, one of them an Australian tourist, received two-year prison sentences, and the presiding judge described the acts in terms that Human Rights Watch cited alongside Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination when it called for the charges to be dropped and the men released.

Arrests ended before the statute changed. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested, four years before decriminalisation took legal effect.

The 2013 Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation. The Asia Pacific Alliance's 2023 policy brief on legal gender recognition describes that pairing as unique worldwide, and treats it as the central legal fact for trans people in Fiji. Fiji was, with South Africa, one of the first two countries to enshrine sexual-orientation non-discrimination in a constitution in 1997; the 2013 text reinstated and expanded the protection.

The constitutional guarantee has no implementing legislation. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker, do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, and leave trans people without an administrative route to have their documents match their presentation. The Asia Pacific Alliance records the resulting marginalisation and discrimination as documented rather than theoretical, and the same brief notes that the constitutional protection operates without a mechanism of enforcement for trans people specifically.

There is no relationship recognition for same-sex couples. The Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as between one man and one woman, and no civil-union or equivalent status exists.

Outright International's country overview adds three further features of the current regime: employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2007; health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation; and organisations working on these issues cannot register. Intersex bodily autonomy is not protected in law.
